question: Which elements must a California notary seal contain?

options.text: The State Seal, the words 'Notary Public', the notary's name, county of principal place of business, commission expiration date, commission number and the manufacturer/vendor ID number
options.why: Correct. §8207 lists the State Seal, 'Notary Public', name, county of principal place of business, expiration date, commission number and manufacturer ID number.

options.text: A five-pointed star and the notary's ID number only
options.why: Wrong. A five-pointed star and an ID number describe the Texas seal.
Wrong. A home address isn't a seal element.
Wrong. The name alone leaves out the other required elements.

explanation: Government Code §8207 lists the State Seal, 'Notary Public', name, county, expiration date, commission number and manufacturer ID number.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: What are the size limits for a California seal?

options.text: Circular: no more than 2 inches in diameter; rectangular: no more than 1 inch by 2½ inches
options.why: Correct. §8207 limits a circular seal to 2 inches in diameter and a rectangular seal to 1 by 2½ inches.
Wrong. There are size limits.
Wrong. A 3-inch round seal exceeds the 2-inch limit.
Wrong. A 1-inch square isn't one of the specified shapes or limits.

explanation: A circular seal may be up to 2 inches; a rectangular seal up to 1 by 2½ inches.

question: What border must the seal have?

options.why: Correct. §8207 requires a serrated or milled-edge border.
Wrong. A border is required.
Wrong. A star border isn't specified.
Wrong. Gold foil isn't required.

explanation: The seal must have a serrated or milled-edge border.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: The seal impression must be:

options.why: Correct. §8207 requires the impression to be photographically reproducible so it shows on scanned and recorded copies.
Wrong. An embossed-only impression doesn't reproduce photographically.
Wrong. Pencil isn't permanent and can't make a seal impression.
Wrong. An invisible seal would defeat its purpose.

explanation: The seal must be photographically reproducible.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: How must the seal be kept?

options.text: In a locked and secured area under the notary's direct and exclusive control
options.why: Correct. §8207 requires the seal to be kept in a locked, secured area under the notary's direct and exclusive control.
Wrong. A shared drawer lets others use the seal.
Wrong. The employer must not control the seal.
Wrong. Security is required.

explanation: The seal must be kept locked and under the notary's direct and exclusive control.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: Before a vendor may make a California notary seal, what must the notary obtain?

options.text: A Certificate of Authorization to Manufacture a Notary Public Seal from the Secretary of State
options.why: Correct. Under §8207.3, a vendor may make a seal only after the Secretary of State issues a Certificate of Authorization to Manufacture.
Wrong. An employer's letter doesn't authorize making a seal.
Wrong. A business license isn't the required authorization.
Wrong. The Certificate of Authorization is required.

explanation: A seal can only be made after the Secretary of State issues a Certificate of Authorization to Manufacture.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207.3 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: A notary's seal is lost. What must they do?

options.text: Immediately notify the Secretary of State
options.why: Correct. A lost, stolen, destroyed or damaged seal must be reported to the Secretary of State immediately.

options.text: Buy a new one without reporting
options.why: Wrong. A replacement can't be made without reporting and a new authorization.
Wrong. Using another notary's seal is fraud.
Wrong. A hand-drawn seal isn't valid.

explanation: Loss of the seal must be reported to the Secretary of State immediately.

question: What should a notary do with the seal when the commission ends without renewal?

options.why: Correct. When a commission ends without renewal, the notary destroys the seal so no one can misuse it.
Wrong. Keeping an active-looking seal risks misuse.
Wrong. Giving it to the employer invites misuse.
Wrong. Selling a seal invites fraud.

explanation: On resignation, revocation or expiration, the notary destroys the seal.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: May anyone other than the notary use the seal?

options.why: Correct. Only the commissioned notary may use their seal.
Wrong. Employers may never use the seal.
Wrong. Each notary uses only their own seal.
Wrong. Family members may never use the seal.

explanation: Only the notary may use their seal.

question: The seal impression is smudged and illegible on a document. What should the notary do?

options.text: Place a new, clear impression nearby without covering the original, if appropriate, and never alter the bad one
options.why: Correct. Add a clear new impression nearby without covering the original, and never alter the smudged one.
Wrong. Drawing over an impression alters it.
Wrong. An unreadable seal can get the document rejected.
Wrong. Correction fluid alters the official impression.

explanation: If an impression is unreadable, a clear new impression may be placed nearby; never alter the original.
source: Cal. Sec. of State Notary Public Handbook

question: What county appears on a California seal?

options.text: The county of the notary's principal place of business
options.why: Correct. The seal shows the county of the notary's principal place of business on file.

options.text: The county where each act takes place
options.why: Wrong. The county where each act happens goes in the venue, not on the seal.
Wrong. Birthplace isn't a seal element.
Wrong. There's no rule that every seal shows Sacramento.

explanation: The seal shows the county of the notary's principal place of business.

question: Is the seal required on California notarial certificates?

options.why: Correct. The seal authenticates every notarial certificate.
Wrong. The seal is required.
Wrong. Every certificate needs the seal, not only deeds.
Wrong. Every certificate needs the seal, wherever the document will be used.

explanation: Notarial certificates require the notary's seal.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: What is the civil penalty for failing to keep the seal secure?

options.why: Correct. §8214.21 provides a civil penalty of up to $1,500 for failing to secure the seal.
Wrong. $25 understates the penalty.
Wrong. $50,000 is far above the cap.
Wrong. The statute does impose a penalty.

explanation: Failure to secure the seal carries a civil penalty of up to $1,500.

question: After a name change, may the notary keep using the old seal?

options.text: No; after filing the amendment, a new seal reflecting the new name is required
options.why: Correct. After the name-change amendment, the notary needs a new seal showing the new name.
Wrong. The old seal no longer matches the commission.

options.text: Yes, with the name crossed out
options.why: Wrong. Altering a seal by crossing out the name isn't allowed.
Wrong. There's no exception for relatives.

explanation: A new seal is needed after the name change is processed.

question: What is the manufacturer or vendor ID number on the seal for?

options.text: To identify the authorized seal maker
options.why: Correct. The manufacturer or vendor ID number identifies the authorized maker of the seal.
Wrong. It isn't a phone number.
Wrong. It isn't the bond number.
Wrong. It's a required element, not decoration.

explanation: The manufacturer or vendor ID number identifies who made the seal.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8207 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 34)

question: Should a seal impression cover text or signatures?

options.why: Correct. The seal must not cover text or signatures, which would make both illegible.
Wrong. Covering text obscures the document's content.
Wrong. Covering the notary's signature makes it unreadable.
Wrong. Placement rules apply to every document, not only deeds.

explanation: Place the seal so it doesn't cover text or signatures.
source: Cal. Sec. of State Notary Public Handbook
